anatomy.intro: Four structures that explain the form of 'Fukurokuryuzinboku'.

parts.function: An unusually swollen section of rib creates the cultivar's distinctive shape.
parts.label: Rounded lobe

parts.function: This small cushion carries the short spine cluster.
parts.label: Areole

parts.function: Spines defend the otherwise exposed succulent surface.
parts.label: Short spine

parts.function: New stem tissue extends the column and continues its lumpy rib pattern.
parts.label: Growing tip

flowers.text: LLIFLE describes greenish-white flowers only about 2.5–3.7 cm across for this cultivar. Their modest size contrasts with the exaggerated stem shape; a small indoor plant may be enjoyed for its form alone.

growth.note: This is irregular cultivated growth, so symmetry and a precise annual height gain are not expectations.

stages.text: A young plant displays only a few swollen rib sections.
stages.title: Short rooted column

stages.text: Upward growth adds successive rounded projections.
stages.title: Repeated lobes

stages.text: Older stems can thicken and branch into a more substantial plant.
stages.title: Larger framework

habitat.text: Myrtillocactus geometrizans is a Mexican tree cactus of desert and dry shrubland. 'Fukurokuryuzinboku' is a cultivated monstrose form, not a separate wild species. Its repeated rounded swellings reshape the normal ribs, while the blue-green stem and widely spaced spine cushions retain the underlying species' recognizable character.

lookalikes.name: Variegated blue torch
lookalikes.text: Blue torch keeps comparatively straight ribs, with pale cream color sectors. This cultivar's key feature is swollen rib shape.

mature.text: The normal species can become a branching tree around 4 m tall in suitable cultivation. The monstrose cultivar has a different outline and pace, so that figure is background rather than a predicted indoor height.

milestones.text: Purchased at Carlsons' Greenhouse in a 3-inch individual pot.
milestones.title: Joined the collection

nameStory.text: The species was described as Cereus geometrizans in 1837 and moved to Myrtillocactus in 1897; the cultivated shape is a later horticultural selection.
